concepts.name: virtual reality
concepts.definition: Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.

The early era in the historical evolution of virtual reality (VR) is the period before modern digital computers were developed in the 1940s, and although not everything was present in that era, a few key developments were conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality experiences.

In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

The flight simulator concept introduced for the first time in 1928 by Edwin A. Link evolved into sophisticated flight simulators with multiple sensors that provide an immersive experience, and this early development is considered a precursor to modern multi-sensory immersive virtual reality (VR).

The main objective of any virtual reality (VR) system is to let the user experience an artificial environment through sensory stimuli provided by the computer, not only for sight and sound but for all sensory organs.

There are broadly two major issues in experiencing virtual reality (VR): the technological issue of how to generate suitable sensory stimuli for the artificial environment, and the psychological issue of how to perceive those stimuli suitably, a human-factor issue that technology does not address and that is likely to differ between users.

The technological and psychological issues in virtual reality (VR) give rise to two major concerns that appear in almost every literature on VR technology or experience, namely immersion and presence.
The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

Cyber sickness can be independent of age when users view general virtual reality (VR) content, while age may be a factor for controllable content, making the age relationship clearer for controllable content.

A possible reason for increased cyber sickness among female head-mounted display (HMD) users is inter-pupillary distance (IPD) fit, because IPD determines stereoscopic vision and a greater proportion of females may have trouble finding a good fit; this implies virtual reality (VR) displays should have a wider IPD adjustable range for female users.

Virtual reality (VR) recreates realistic movement and visual environments, making the user feel as if in a real-world environment; therefore, users with motion sickness (MS) susceptibility tend also to have cyber sickness susceptibility.

Prior exposure to virtual reality (VR) systems and repeated exposure to VR can reduce the effect of motion sickness (MS) susceptibility on cyber sickness and reduce cyber sickness severity over time, so the positive correlation may not hold if either or both conditions are satisfied.

A user's physical position affects cyber sickness susceptibility: using a virtual reality (VR) system in a standing posture is likely to induce more cyber sickness, or more severe cyber sickness, than using the same system while sitting.

A virtual reality (VR) system is designed to create interactions that make the user feel immersed, and the amount of presence and the quality of the overall experience depend on fooling the user's perceptual system into believing the virtual system is the familiar real world.
Virtual reality generally provides the brain with sensory signals that are inconsistent with the user's real-life experiences and behavior.

One possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body adapts to the new stimuli, making the user unaware of any flaws in the system and causing the user to believe that the virtual system is the real world rather than an artificial system.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.
An understanding of human perception is needed to design a better virtual reality (VR) system or to identify and resolve flaws in a given system.

In the Unity editor interface, the preference tab lets the developer select extended reality (XR) settings for three system types: virtual reality, which simulates a completely artificial environment around the user; mixed reality, which combines Unity's own environment with the user's real world environment and allows the environments to interact; and augmented reality, which provides layers of content over a digital view of the real world.

concepts.name: head-mounted display
concepts.definition: A head-mounted display (HMD) is a wearable, mobile visual display that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components and uses one or two small screens directly in front of the user's eyes to place images for monoscopic or stereoscopic viewing. It can be non-see-through, optical see-through, or video see-through.

defining_facts.text: The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s.

In the 1950s, especially toward the latter half of the decade, people started working on and considering different types of head-mounted displays (HMDs), a new kind of computer display that was less common than regular computer monitors.
In 1961, engineers at Philco Corporation developed an early head-mounted display (HMD) that could track users' motion but was bulky and uncomfortable to wear.
In 1965, Tom Furness and colleagues at the Wright-Patterson Air Force Base worked on visually coupled systems for pilots that consisted of head-mounted displays (HMDs).
In 1967, Sutherland developed the Sword of Damocles, a head-mounted display (HMD), and was the first to demonstrate an HMD with head tracking and computer-generated imagery.

In 1985, Scott Fisher and colleagues at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) developed and launched Virtual Visual Environment Display (VIVED), the first commercially viable and commercially available stereoscopic head-tracked head-mounted display (HMD) with a wide field of view.

The three broad types of visual displays are head-mounted displays (HMDs), which are wearable and mobile, world-fixed displays, which are not wearable and are stationary, and regular displays, which are mobile or can be stationary.
Although head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be used as input to track head motion, their primary use is as a display device.
A head-mounted display (HMD) is a sophisticated piece of equipment that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components within its package.

A head-mounted display (HMD) places images directly in front of the user's eyes using one or two small screens, with one screen providing monoscopic viewing and two screens providing stereoscopic viewing, and stereoscopic HMDs are more common than monoscopic HMDs.
Head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be further categorized into three types: non-see-through, optical see-through, and video see-through.

Non-see-through HMDs are typically used in virtual reality (VR), optical see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented reality (AR), and video see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented virtuality, in which real-world images or videos appear in real time within an artificial or virtual environment.

concepts.name: virtual environment
concepts.definition: Virtual environment is a non-real, computer-generated graphical representation of a real or imaginary world, populated with artificial objects, that is experienced through computer-generated sensory stimuli.

defining_facts.text: A virtual reality (VR) system is defined by three characteristics: an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment; a system with these aspects can be categorized as a virtual reality system and distinguished from other systems, which are not supposed to have these aspects.

The artificial or synthetic environment of a virtual reality (VR) system is a computer-generated graphical representation of a real world or an imaginary or fantastic world, populated with artificial objects, and is not a real environment.

An artificial environment in a virtual reality (VR) system can recreate a real world using real-world imagery or video, as in a virtual tour, but it still counts as a virtual reality system because it is a computer-generated scenario and changes are not happening in real time.

The sensory experience characteristic of a virtual reality (VR) system means that the system provides computer-generated stimuli to the user's sensory organs, such as eyes and ears, so the user can immersively experience the artificial or synthetic environment, and this immersive experience is a hallmark of a virtual reality system.

The user interaction characteristic of a virtual reality (VR) system means that the system must be interactive: the user can act on or interact with elements in the environment, and user actions or inputs partially determine what happens in the environment, producing dynamic changes in the virtual environment, just as people interact with objects in the real world.

concepts.name: field of view
concepts.definition: Field of view (FOV) is an angular measure of the region visible to the eye at a single point in time, and in virtual reality it is the amount of virtual environment visible.

defining_facts.text: Field of view (FOV) is a content-related factor in virtual reality (VR) that affects susceptibility to cybersickness (CS), and it is the extent to which the display in a VR headset captures the user's field of vision.
A larger field of view (FOV) in virtual reality (VR) captures a larger field of vision and generally results in greater immersion.
Research has found that reducing the field of view (FOV) in virtual reality (VR) can be an effective way to alleviate symptoms of cybersickness (CS).

An excessively narrow field of view (FOV) in virtual reality (VR) can decrease immersion and increase head movement to look for things in the environment, which may exacerbate or increase cybersickness (CS); finding the optimal FOV is crucial for creating a comfortable VR experience.

Developer-side strategies for reducing cybersickness (CS) include field of view (FOV) adjustment, dynamic visual blur, rest frames, optical-flow manipulation, hardware-level alterations, and locomotion modifications.
Field of view (FOV) is the amount of virtual environment that is visible at any moment.
Field of view (FOV) adjustment can, ideally, mitigate the onset or severity of cybersickness (CS) because restricting the field of view reduces peripheral optical flow.
Field of view (FOV) adjustment has been found to be effective across genders without any negative impacts.

A drawback of field of view (FOV) adjustment is that it can reduce presence or sense of presence and impair performance in visual tasks because it restricts certain visual content, potentially degrading user experience.
A symmetric mask is a classical field of view (FOV) adjustment technique that occludes the periphery in reaction to translational and/or angular velocity, but it can affect presence.

An asymmetric mask is a field of view (FOV) adjustment strategy that is considered an adaptive restrictor because it obscures peripheral regions with higher optical flow during virtual locomotion while leaving regions with lower optical flow visible, so it adapts based on optical flow.

A side restrictor, described as an asymmetric mask, is a field of view (FOV) adjustment strategy that obscures only one side of the periphery during virtual rotation and laterally shifts the center of restriction in the direction of the turn, providing a controlled way of restriction.
A ground visible restrictor is a field of view (FOV) adjustment strategy in which the ground plane remains visible during movement.

Optical-flow manipulation is a cybersickness (CS) reduction technique that can involve visually mixing optical-flow patterns in the reverse direction of virtual visual motion, using a restricted field of view (FOV) aligned with optical flow, or reducing perceived optical flow by geometrical simplification of the virtual environment.
Field of view (FOV) is the view frustum, that is, the region visible to the human eye, and it is an angular measure of what can be seen at a single point in time.

The human eye has an approximately 180-degree horizontal field of view (FOV) and a 150-degree vertical field of view, and within the 180-degree horizontal range a person sees things using both central and peripheral vision.

concepts.name: presence
concepts.definition: Presence is a subjective psychological state in which an experience generated by human-made technology is perceived as real, because the user fails to acknowledge the technology's role and perceives computer-generated stimuli as coming from the real world.

defining_facts.text: Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.

Presence is defined by the International Society for Presence Research, which has had the definition since 2000, as a psychological state or subjective perception in which part or all of an individual's current experience is generated by or filtered through human-made technology, but part or all of the individual's perception fails to accurately acknowledge the role of the technology in the experience.

Presence is a state in which computer-generated stimuli stimulate the user's sensory organs, and the user's perception is as good as perceiving reality because the user cannot distinguish those stimuli from real-world stimuli, so the user perceives them as coming from the real world rather than from a computer.

Presence is a state of consciousness or psychological sense of being in the virtual environment that exists inside the user's mind, has no direct manifestation, is difficult to measure objectively, and therefore requires the user's subjective experience to be taken into account.

Presence can be a function of both the user's subjective experience and a system's immersion, that is the objective or technological experience, so immersion can aid an enhanced perception of presence and is capable of producing presence, but it does not ensure presence.

Presence can be limited by immersion, and the greater the immersion a system or application provides, the greater the potential for a user to feel present in the virtual world, while the lesser the immersive technology provides, the lesser the presence.

The overall goal of any virtual reality system is to create a high degree of presence, that is to make users feel that they are really in the virtual world and unable to distinguish the real world from the virtual world.
Creating a high degree of presence in a virtual reality system requires the system to provide a high degree of immersion, and this requirement is a systemic issue.

The goal of any virtual reality (VR) system is to create a high degree of presence, meaning that people believe they are in the real world while they are actually in a virtual world, and the closer a VR system is to this goal, the better the immersive experience it provides.

Cybersickness (CS) mitigation involves a trade-off between reducing cybersickness and preserving user experience, because mitigation strategies often affect presence or the user's ability to perceive the virtual world, and presence affects user experience.

Mark Weiser's quote that the most profound technologies are those that disappear and presence refer to the same thing: the technological aspect surrounding the user should disappear from the user's perception, and the goal is to build systems that do not make it apparent that the user is using a specialized technological product.

In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the interaction and the perceptual stimuli, the latter being the output generated by the system, are designed to create the best possible illusion of reality, not actual reality, in order to enhance presence, which is a sense of reality as if the user is in the real world.

Presence in a virtual environment requires both reinforcing the virtual experience as believable and developing attachment to that experience, and the auditory experience plays a very important role in increasing presence in the virtual environment.

The key concerns to be addressed in the Majuli Island virtual reality (VR) Tour are capturing both the tangible and intangible aspects of the island's cultural heritage, which is the broader objective, the user experience, specifically the extent to which users feel present in the virtual island, and minimizing the risk of cyber sickness while users explore the island.
Presence is a psychological state of mind that is measured by standard questionnaires.
The QEP questionnaire was used to measure presence, and it is a 2004 revised version of the standard presence questionnaire (PQ).

The presence measure used to evaluate the virtual tour of Majuli Island included involvement, interface quality, adaptation or immersion, and visual fidelity, and tangible and intangible reconstruction fidelity was additionally reported for participants who had previously visited Majuli Island.

The overall user presence ratings for the virtual tour of Majuli Island were involvement mean 5.65 (standard deviation 1.11, coefficient of variation 0.19), interface quality mean 4.37 (standard deviation 1.4, coefficient of variation 0.32), adaptation and immersion mean 5.4 (standard deviation 1.13, coefficient of variation 0.2), and visual fidelity mean 5.79 (standard deviation 0.93, coefficient of variation 0.16).

The presence ratings for participants who had previously visited Majuli Island were tangible and intangible reconstruction fidelity mean 5.68 (standard deviation 1, coefficient of variation 0.177), involvement mean 5.83 (standard deviation 1.05, coefficient of variation 0.18), interface quality mean 4.72 (standard deviation 1.36, coefficient of variation 0.33), adaptation or immersion mean 5.61 (standard deviation 1.15, coefficient of variation 0.22), and visual fidelity mean 5.94 (standard deviation 0.93, coefficient of variation 0.15).

The overall presence results for the virtual tour of Majuli Island were summarized as good presence, meaning that users felt reasonably well located within the virtual environment while virtually exploring Majuli Island.

concepts.name: cybersickness
concepts.definition: Cybersickness (CS) is a condition primarily relevant to virtual reality that may be caused by multiple internal and external factors and in which a user may experience symptoms such as nausea, dizziness, headache, or disorientation.

defining_facts.text: Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.

A large number of symptoms may indicate the onset of cybersickness (CS) or cybersickness itself, and common ones include nausea, headache, excessive sweating, dryness of mouth, fullness of stomach, vomiting or a tendency to vomit, dizziness, disorientation, fatigue, and strange hand-eye coordination in which coordination does not happen in the expected way, so if one or more of these symptoms occur during a virtual reality (VR) experience, cybersickness can be assumed to be happening or going to happen.
Cybersickness (CS) can be caused by many factors, not by a single factor.

Reducing the impact of cybersickness (CS) is very important for usability and acceptability of virtual reality (VR) systems because it greatly enhances overall user experience and makes virtual reality applications more appealing to a wider range of people.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.

A sensory mismatch in a virtual reality (VR) system may be insignificant if the user's brain can adapt, but for other users it can cause cybersickness, with symptoms such as fatigue, headache, dizziness, and nausea.

Cybersickness, also known as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR), and it is not a single-factor effect because a variety of factors can affect it.

The factors that can induce cybersickness are broadly divided into internal factors, which include the age of the user, the gender of the user, the user's susceptibility to motion sickness, the physical condition of the user, and the emotional condition of the user, and external factors, which include hardware factors such as display resolution, latency, latency jitter, type of display, and type of input, and virtual reality (VR) content factors such as visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.

Finding feasible solutions to reduce the impact of cybersickness while a user is experiencing virtual reality (VR) is important because it is supposed to greatly enhance overall user experience and make VR more appealing to a wider range of people.

Cybersickness mitigation strategies often come at the cost of presence because reducing cybersickness may make the user feel more in an artificial environment than in a real environment and less likely to obtain a proper immersive experience.

concepts.name: teleportation
concepts.definition: Teleportation is a virtual reality locomotion operation in which a user selects a virtual target location and the virtual viewpoint instantly changes from the current location to that target, without physical movement.

defining_facts.text: The type of transition, meaning how the scene changes from one field of view to another, is another aspect of locomotion that affects cybersickness (CS); teleportation, an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic free movement such as walking, running, and jumping.

Teleportation in virtual reality (VR) is a locomotion operation in which a user can pull up a menu, point to a desired virtual location, and be sent to that location without making any physical movement.

Target selection-based locomotion techniques include teleportation, which instantly changes the virtual viewpoint from the current location to the target location, map dragging, in which the user fixes a location to move there instantly, and the jumper technique in cave-type systems.

Route planning-based locomotion is a selection-based locomotion technique in which the user selects a route to the target rather than only the endpoint; there may be multiple routes, and while moving through the selected route, different viewpoint changes make the user feel movement along a path, providing more granular control over travel and slightly more natural movement than target-based teleportation.

Teleportation-type movement in a virtual world can be the best choice for reducing overall exposure duration because it provides instantaneous movement between two points at maximum speed, but it is not a natural movement and may not always be a good approach when naturalness is required.

concepts.name: questionnaire-based input
concepts.definition: Questionnaire-based input is a subjective input for measuring cybersickness that generally takes the form of ratings of users' discomfort or disorientation on a numerical scale.

defining_facts.text: Inputs for measuring cybersickness (CS) can be questionnaire-based, physiological and biometric information, behavioral information, and content-based information.

Questionnaire-based input for measuring cybersickness (CS) is a common method that uses self-report questionnaires or scales, generally in the form of ratings, to rate users' discomfort or disorientation on a numerical scale.
Questionnaire-based cybersickness (CS) scales are easy to administer and help researchers or practitioners better understand the causes of cybersickness and identify potential interventions.

Questionnaire-based cybersickness (CS) scales are typically administered before or after an experience, can also be administered during the experience, with before and after being the most common timing and during being occasional.

concepts.name: sickness score
concepts.definition: A sickness score is a numerical output of cybersickness measurement that quantifies the severity of the cybersickness experience and is generally produced by a regression model in machine learning-based evaluation.

defining_facts.text: The output of cybersickness (CS) measurement can be binary classes, multiple classes, or a sickness score that is a number.
Machine learning (ML)-based cybersickness (CS) evaluation can produce either classification labels or a numerical sickness score as output.
In machine learning (ML)-based cybersickness (CS) evaluation, a sickness score quantifies the severity of the cybersickness experience and is generally produced by a regression model.

concepts.name: physiological input
concepts.definition: Physiological input is an input used to detect cybersickness, because questionnaire-based inputs can be subjective, inaccurate, and not always reliable.

defining_facts.text: Physiological or biometric inputs can be used to detect cybersickness (CS) because questionnaire-based inputs can be subjective, are prone to inaccuracies, and may not always be reliable.
Electroencephalogram (EEG) is one of the widely used physiological or biometric inputs for detecting cybersickness (CS).

Physiological or biometric inputs for detecting cybersickness (CS) include heart rate, galvanic skin response (GSR), electroencephalogram (EEG), electrocardiogram (ECG), electrogastrogram (EGG), electrooculography (EOG), respiration signals, photoplethysmography (PPG), and electromyogram (EMG).

concepts.name: optical flow
concepts.definition: Optical flow is the apparent motion perceived by virtual reality users due to relative motion between the user and the environment.

defining_facts.text: Content-based inputs for measuring cybersickness (CS) include optical flow, depth cues, and exceptional motion velocity.
Optical flow is the apparent motion perceived by virtual reality (VR) users due to relative motion between the user and the environment.

concepts.name: machine learning-based cybersickness evaluation
concepts.definition: Machine learning-based cybersickness evaluation is an input-based cybersickness measurement technique that uses automated algorithms trained on psychological, physiological, or biometric inputs to automatically determine cybersickness, producing classification labels or a numerical sickness score.

defining_facts.text: Cybersickness (CS) measurement techniques based on input are broadly of two types: manual evaluation, which is based on human intervention, and machine learning-based (ML) or automated evaluation, which uses automated algorithms on input to measure cybersickness.
Machine learning-based (ML) evaluation of cybersickness (CS) can use psychological, physiological, or biometric inputs to train models that automatically determine cybersickness.

One way to perform machine learning-based (ML) evaluation of cybersickness (CS) is to use transparent models, which provide clear insight into the decision-making process and whose inner workings can easily be understood.

concepts.name: transparent model
concepts.definition: A transparent model is a model used for machine learning-based evaluation of cybersickness that provides clear insight into its decision-making process and whose inner workings can be easily understood.

defining_facts.text: One way to perform machine learning-based (ML) evaluation of cybersickness (CS) is to use transparent models, which provide clear insight into the decision-making process and whose inner workings can easily be understood.
Stepwise regression analysis can be considered a transparent model that is utilized to measure cybersickness (CS) using a variety of physiological signals or physiological inputs.

never_defined.name: user experience
never_defined.definition: User experience is a key concern in virtual reality system design that is enhanced by reducing cybersickness, affected by presence, and supported by wayfinding and environment design.

never_defined.name: cyber sickness susceptibility
never_defined.definition: Cyber sickness susceptibility is a user's susceptibility to cyber sickness that is related to age, motion sickness susceptibility, retinal eccentricity, and physical position, and can be measured with questionnaires.

never_defined.name: cybersickness severity
never_defined.definition: Cybersickness severity is the level of cybersickness that postural sway can indicate and that self-report scores or ratings, machine-learning classification labels, or sickness scores can assess or quantify.

never_defined.name: angular velocity
never_defined.definition: Angular velocity is what a gyroscope captures in an inertial measurement unit, and sensor tracking relies mainly on its readings.

never_defined.name: electroencephalogram
never_defined.definition: An Electroencephalogram (EEG) is one of the widely used physiological or biometric inputs for detecting cybersickness.

never_defined.name: depth cue
never_defined.definition: A depth cue is a cue in human vision that is used as a content-based input for measuring cybersickness.

never_defined.name: CN2 rule induction
never_defined.definition: CN2 rule induction is one of the interpretable machine learning algorithms used to measure cybersickness.

never_defined.name: bagged decision tree
never_defined.definition: The bagged decision tree is one of the interpretable machine learning algorithms used to measure cybersickness.

never_defined.name: Naive Bayes classifier
never_defined.definition: A Naive Bayes classifier is an interpretable machine learning algorithm used to measure cybersickness.

never_defined.name: K-nearest neighbors
never_defined.definition: K-nearest neighbors (KNN) is an interpretable machine learning algorithm used to measure, predict, or classify cybersickness.

never_defined.name: linear discriminant analysis
never_defined.definition: Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) is an interpretable machine learning algorithm used to measure cybersickness.

never_defined.name: long short-term memory
never_defined.definition: Long short-term memory (LSTM) is a machine learning model used to measure or evaluate cybersickness.

never_defined.name: explainable boosting machine
never_defined.definition: Explainable boosting machine (EBM) is a machine learning technique that can be combined with other machine learning techniques to identify and provide insight into cybersickness.

never_defined.name: decision tree
never_defined.definition: A decision tree is a machine learning technique that has been used in combinations, with biophysiological and subjective measurements as input, to identify and provide insight into cybersickness.

never_defined.name: logistic regression
never_defined.definition: Logistic regression is a machine learning technique used in combinations or hybrid models to identify, predict, or classify cybersickness.

never_defined.name: convolutional neural network
never_defined.definition: A convolutional neural network (CNN) is a black-box model studied for cybersickness evaluation, with a specialized form for electroencephalography prediction.

never_defined.name: support vector machine
never_defined.definition: Support vector machine (SVM) is a black-box model for cybersickness evaluation and measurement.

never_defined.name: prediction accuracy
never_defined.definition: Prediction accuracy is a property of cybersickness evaluation models.

never_defined.name: deep embedded self-organizing map
never_defined.definition: Deep embedded self-organizing map (DESOM) is part of hybrid models used to predict or classify cybersickness.

never_defined.name: autoencoder
never_defined.definition: An Autoencoder is a component of hybrid models used to predict or classify cybersickness.

never_defined.name: electroencephalogram network
never_defined.definition: Electroencephalogram network (EEGNET) is a specialized convolutional neural network for electroencephalography prediction.

never_defined.name: voting classifier
never_defined.definition: A voting classifier is a classifier included in hybrid models for predicting or classifying cybersickness, combining random forest, K-nearest neighbors (KNN), logistic regression, and a multilayer perceptron neural network for binary and three-level classification.

never_defined.name: random forest
never_defined.definition: Random forest is one of the methods combined in a voting classifier used for binary or three-level classification of cybersickness.

never_defined.name: multilayer perceptron
never_defined.definition: A multilayer perceptron is a neural network used in a voting classifier for binary and three-level classification in hybrid models that predict or classify cybersickness.

never_defined.name: cybersickness evaluation technique
never_defined.definition: Cybersickness evaluation technique is a technique for evaluating cybersickness, and a classification based on the event of measurement distinguishes detection from prediction.

never_defined.name: mitigation measures
never_defined.definition: Mitigation measures are measures that can be enabled before cybersickness occurs.

never_defined.name: video features
never_defined.definition: Video features are used in limited machine-learning research to predict susceptibility to cybersickness or impending cybersickness episodes.

never_defined.name: baseline measurements
never_defined.definition: Baseline measurements are measurements taken before virtual reality immersion and used in limited research on predicting cybersickness.

never_defined.name: cybersickness episode
never_defined.definition: A cybersickness episode is an episode of cybersickness that can be impending and may be predicted by machine learning studies.

never_defined.name: score
never_defined.definition: A score is a rating-scale output of self-report questionnaires for cybersickness and can be used to assess the severity of cybersickness.

never_defined.name: rating
never_defined.definition: A rating is one of the outputs of self-report questionnaires for cybersickness that can be used to assess the severity of cybersickness.

never_defined.name: rating scale
never_defined.definition: A rating scale is a scale used to collect user feedback or self-report data as scores or ratings, such as a 1-to-10 scale where 1 is worst and 10 is best.

never_defined.name: classification label
never_defined.definition: A classification label is an output of machine learning-based cybersickness evaluation that indicates the likelihood or severity of cybersickness.

never_defined.name: regression model
never_defined.definition: A regression model is generally used in machine learning-based cybersickness evaluation to produce a sickness score that quantifies the severity of the cybersickness experience.

never_defined.name: developer perspective
never_defined.definition: Developer perspective is one of the important perspectives from which cybersickness mitigation is considered, together with the user's perspective.

never_defined.name: user perspective
never_defined.definition: The user perspective is one of the two important perspectives from which cybersickness mitigation is considered.

never_defined.name: peripheral optical flow
never_defined.definition: Peripheral optical flow is reduced by restricting the field of view, an adjustment that can, ideally, mitigate the onset or severity of cybersickness.

never_defined.name: translational velocity
never_defined.definition: Translational velocity is a velocity that, with or without angular velocity, can make a symmetric mask occlude the periphery in a field of view adjustment technique.

never_defined.name: adaptive restrictor
never_defined.definition: An adaptive restrictor is a field of view adjustment strategy that adapts based on optical flow by obscuring peripheral regions with higher optical flow during virtual locomotion while leaving regions with lower optical flow visible.

never_defined.name: ground plane
never_defined.definition: Ground plane is a plane that remains visible during movement in a ground visible restrictor.

never_defined.name: depth-of-field blur
never_defined.definition: Depth-of-field blur is a type of dynamic visual blur, a technique for reducing the possibility of cybersickness, that uses well-known depth cues in human vision.

never_defined.name: peripheral blur
never_defined.definition: Peripheral blur is a type of dynamic visual blur, a technique for reducing the possibility of cybersickness.

never_defined.name: head reference frame
never_defined.definition: Head reference frame is a reference frame to which rest frames in a virtual environment can be attached.

never_defined.name: virtual nose
never_defined.definition: Virtual nose is an example of an independent visual background, a rest frame attached to the head reference frame.

never_defined.name: perceived optical flow
never_defined.definition: Perceived optical flow is the virtual visual motion that optical-flow manipulation can reduce by geometrical simplification of the virtual environment.

never_defined.name: geometrical simplification
never_defined.definition: Geometrical simplification is used to reduce perceived optical flow in a virtual environment as part of a cybersickness reduction technique.

never_defined.name: light-emitting diode matrix
never_defined.definition: Light-emitting diode matrix is used in a sparse peripheral display that expands the periphery of a head-mounted display as a hardware-level alteration for reducing cybersickness.

never_defined.name: light-emitting diode screen
never_defined.definition: A Light-emitting diode screen is a miniature screen placed in a head-mounted display, used in hardware-level alterations for reducing cybersickness.

never_defined.name: Noble camera setup twin cam
never_defined.definition: A Noble camera setup twin cam is a hardware-level alteration used to reduce motion blur and cybersickness.

never_defined.name: motion blur
never_defined.definition: Motion blur is one of the things reduced by a hardware-level camera setup used to reduce cybersickness.

never_defined.name: hybrid 360 panoramic video camera rig
never_defined.definition: A Hybrid 360 panoramic video camera rig is a hardware-level alteration that can be used to reduce cybersickness.

never_defined.name: haptic cue
never_defined.definition: A haptic cue is an alternating cue synchronized to users' footsteps that is applied using additional hardware in a hardware-level alteration to reduce cybersickness.

never_defined.name: whole-body tactile feedback
never_defined.definition: Whole-body tactile feedback is vibration-driven tactile feedback used in floor vibrations to match the vibrations of a virtual environment.

never_defined.name: simultaneous presentation of sound and vibration
never_defined.definition: Simultaneous presentation of sound and vibration is a hardware-level alteration that has been tried for reducing cybersickness.

never_defined.name: vibration motor
never_defined.definition: A vibration motor is a small motor used for vibrotactile feedback during a walking experience.

never_defined.name: vibrotactile feedback
never_defined.definition: Vibrotactile feedback is feedback provided by vibration motors during a walking experience.

never_defined.name: rotational acceleration
never_defined.definition: Rotational acceleration is produced in short bursts by modified motion platforms to match visual forward acceleration and reduce cybersickness.

never_defined.name: visual forward acceleration
never_defined.definition: Visual forward acceleration is an acceleration that can be matched by short bursts of rotational acceleration in modified motion platforms to reduce cybersickness.

never_defined.name: novel walking method
never_defined.definition: A novel walking method is a locomotion modification for reducing cybersickness, used instead of natural walking.

never_defined.name: natural walking
never_defined.definition: Natural walking is a walking method that can be replaced by novel walking methods in locomotion modifications for reducing cybersickness.

never_defined.name: steering-based locomotion
never_defined.definition: Steering-based locomotion is a type of locomotion technique used to accomplish travel in navigation.

never_defined.name: dynamic steering speed
never_defined.definition: Dynamic steering speed is a locomotion modification for reducing cybersickness, and it skips certain locations when going over long distances to reduce the duration of virtual exposure.

never_defined.name: viewpoint snapping
never_defined.definition: Viewpoint snapping is a locomotion modification for reducing cybersickness that renders moving pictures in discrete chunks during rotation.

never_defined.name: invisible ramp
never_defined.definition: An invisible ramp is a locomotion modification placed on top of stairs for reducing cybersickness.

never_defined.name: developer-side intervention
never_defined.definition: A Developer-side intervention is an intervention for reducing the effects of cybersickness that alone may not be sufficient.

never_defined.name: countermeasure
never_defined.definition: A countermeasure is a user-side measure used to reduce the effects of cybersickness.

never_defined.name: virtual reality session
never_defined.definition: A virtual reality session is an exposure to a virtual environment.

never_defined.name: exposure
never_defined.definition: Exposure is the amount of time users spend in a virtual environment, and longer exposure increases the risk of cybersickness.

never_defined.name: maximum duration
never_defined.definition: Maximum duration is the generally safe upper limit for a virtual reality session that is recommended to reduce cybersickness risk for the majority of users likely to suffer from cybersickness, and the limit may vary with device, content, and other factors.

never_defined.name: diaphragmatic breathing
never_defined.definition: Diaphragmatic breathing is a slow, controlled breathing pattern that users can try to delay the onset, reduce the severity, and, to a large extent, reduce the possibility of cybersickness.

never_defined.name: background music
never_defined.definition: Background music is pleasant music used as a user-side strategy to calm or soothe the mind and reduce cybersickness.

never_defined.name: air flow
never_defined.definition: Air flow is a user-side strategy that can calm or soothe the mind and reduce cybersickness when adequate.

never_defined.name: user-side strategy
never_defined.definition: A User-side strategy is a strategy that can calm or soothe the mind and reduce cybersickness.

introduced.name: classification based on the event of measurement
